analysis.investment_thesis: ACME Solar is a utility company — explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula — and even if we set that aside, it fails on both primary metrics: ROCE of just 8.42% (far below the 20% threshold) and an earnings yield of ~4.4% (EBIT INR 1,237 Cr / EV ~INR 28,164 Cr) with revenue shrinking at -4.6% CAGR. Massive financial leverage (D/E 2.72, borrowings INR 12,998 Cr) absorbs nearly all operating cash flow in finance costs (INR 759 Cr vs EBIT INR 1,237 Cr).
key_strengths: Operating cash flow positive 5/5 years (INR 1,543 Cr in FY25) — plants generate stable contracted revenues
2,540 MW operational capacity with 3,780 MW under construction — scale positions it for future growth if execution holds
65% operating margins reflect the contracted, recurring nature of solar power generation revenue
key_risks: ROIC/ROCE of 8.42% is well below cost of capital in an asset-heavy, capital-intensive business with 2.72x debt-to-equity
FCF deeply negative (-INR 1,719 Cr in FY25) due to massive capex of INR 3,266 Cr — equity dilution or further debt is inevitable
Revenue and EBITDA have been contracting: revenue -4.6% CAGR (FY20-25), EBITDA -9.9% CAGR — the installed base is generating less, not more
red_flags: Utilities sector: explicitly excluded from Magic Formula — regulated returns and capital-intensive structure render EBIT/EV and ROIC metrics incompatible
Finance cost (INR 759 Cr) consumes 61% of EBIT (INR 1,237 Cr) — debt is structurally destroying value for equity holders
Net profit of INR 698 Cr in FY24 included INR 891 Cr other income — strip that out and core earnings are deeply negative
analysis.detailed_analysis:
ACME Solar is a capital-allocation nightmare from a Magic Formula perspective. Utilities are excluded from Greenblatt's framework precisely because their returns are regulated, capital structures are debt-heavy, and ROIC is structurally depressed — ACMESOLAR's 8.42% ROCE illustrates this perfectly. The operating margin of 65% sounds impressive until you realize that finance costs of INR 759 Cr consume most of it, leaving virtually nothing for equity holders.

The growth story is also problematic: EBITDA has declined from INR 2,353 Cr (FY20) to INR 1,396 Cr (FY25) despite the overall renewable energy boom. The company is spending aggressively on new capacity (INR 3,266 Cr capex in FY25) funded by debt (borrowings up from INR 8,536 Cr to INR 12,998 Cr in one year) and fresh equity, generating deeply negative FCF. The FY24 'profit' of INR 698 Cr was largely other income of INR 891 Cr — a one-time item. Stripping that out reveals structural losses. This is an AVOID on every dimension Greenblatt cares about.
